title: Shadow-evaporation self-alignment places bitline and storage contacts without masks
idea: Combine the angled shadow deposition used for Dolan-bridge qubit junctions with the 6F2 cell. The buried-wordline trench topography acts as a built-in stencil, and two directional depositions at +theta and -theta drop the bitline-contact and storage-contact metals on opposite sides of each active pillar.
why: Eliminates 1-2 contact-defining masks and their overlay budget (fact 4); contacts are self-aligned by geometry, giving ~5% cost reduction plus yield gain.

title: Substitute robotic pick-and-place with capillary fluidic self-alignment for die bonding
idea: Dispense a water droplet on a hydrophilic bond site ringed by hydrophobic SAM; a roughly placed DRAM die (+/-50 um) is pulled into <0.5 um alignment by surface tension in milliseconds, the water evaporates, and oxide/Cu hybrid bonding follows. Precision comes from physics, so a coarse gantry can drop >10,000 dies per hour.
why: Fact 6 (HBM stacking tax): hybrid bonders run ~1-2k UPH at $3-5M each; 5-10x throughput cuts stacking capex and misalignment yield loss.

title: MLCC tape-casting lines build high-k capacitor substrates
idea: Worse: fight the 5 fF wall with ever-deeper etched holes. Flip: use the multilayer-ceramic-capacitor industry's tape-cast, co-fired BaTiO3 (k>1000) as the substrate: hundreds of sub-um layers with one via electrode per cell, topped by thin-film access transistors. Charge comes from k, not aspect ratio.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1 needs k~70): k in the thousands, made on low-capex, high-volume MLCC lines.

title: Ni: nickel-stressor spalling makes kerfless substrates without saw slurry
idea: Sputter a tensile Ni stressor film on an ingot face or reclaimed wafer and peel off a 20-50 um single-crystal Si layer by controlled spalling, then smooth it by H2 anneal and bond it to a carrier, skipping wire sawing, lapping and wet polishing.
why: Water and resources: substrate making drops >10x in water, and kerf-free use roughly halves silicon and quartz-crucible demand per wafer (Spruce Pine >80%).

title: Universal pre-patterned array blanks bought like SOI wafers
idea: Inverts 'every DRAM maker patterns its own array front end'. One mega-line with EUV makes standardized 'array blanks' (honeycomb active area plus buried wordlines, the first ~20 critical steps) for all customers; DRAM makers buy blanks like SOI wafers and finish capacitors, periphery and BEOL on DUV-only lines.
why: Concentrates the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) in one fully loaded line, so the rest of industry needs no EUV; scale and utilization could cut litho capital per bit ~30%.

title: Bosch scallop-engineered corrugated capacitor walls double area
idea: Box: Si trench charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x time-multiplexed DRIE with deliberately deep, tuned scallops. Etch/passivation cycle times are set to cut 30-50 nm periodic corrugations, then conformal ALD TiN/high-k/TiN coats them, giving a fixed-depth trench ~1.5-2.5x sidewall area from a recipe timing parameter.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) at lower AR as a recipe-only change on any DRIE; risk is field crowding at corrugation tips raising leakage and scaling scallops below 50 nm holes.

title: Liquid-silane ink laser-annealed into roll-to-roll polysilicon
idea: Magnify printed transistor mobility about 10x by coating cyclopentasilane ink and laser-crystallizing it into polysilicon on the web, giving ~100 cm2/Vs access and sense transistors.
why: Speed of printed memory: makes the printed tier fast enough for near-DRAM latency without vacuum front-end tools.

title: Swappable cartridge chamber liners replace NF3 plasma cleaning
idea: Extreme user: a submarine or habitat fab where no fluorine gas may be stored. Deposition tools get quick-change ceramic/quartz liners that a robot swaps every N wafers; spent liners are cleaned offline by bead blasting or hot KOH, and metal deposits are cleaned in situ with Cl2.
why: PFAS/energy: NF3 is the largest fluorinated-gas use in fabs (high-GWP); tool uptime rises because liner swaps beat long plasma cleans.

title: 77K-cooled AI racks let DRAM drop the high-aspect capacitor module
idea: Extreme user: liquid-nitrogen-immersed AI racks. At 77K junction and GIDL leakage fall ~10^4x, so a ~0.5 fF planar MIM (or the access transistor's own gate/junction capacitance) holds data for seconds; the 60-75:1 pillar etch, its support lattice and 2-3 EUV layers disappear and the cell is built on a 28 nm-class logic flow.
why: Capacitor charge wall + capital: removes ~25-30% of front-end steps and the costliest etch/deposition tools; system cost/bit ~-30% even after cooling overhead, and refresh energy nearly vanishes.

title: Reuse each Czochralski wafer ten times via porous-silicon lift-off
idea: Inverts 'the silicon substrate is consumed'. Anodize a double-layer porous Si film on a prime wafer, grow 2-5 um device-quality epi on it, build the DRAM array, bond to a cheap carrier and split at the porous layer; the prime wafer is repolished and reused ~10x (ELTRAN-style).
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand 5-10x and with it the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint; also hands bonding flows a ready backside.

title: Nanosphere monolayer defines both access pillars and capacitor posts
idea: Box: MIM charge x vertical Si pillar GAA x voltage sense amp x capacitor-over-pillar x Si x Langmuir-Blodgett colloidal monolayer. A close-packed polystyrene sphere layer is O2-plasma shrunk and used to etch hexagonal pillars; after gate ALD and planarization, the exposed pillar tops seed self-aligned capacitor posts, so one self-assembled layer sets the whole lattice with zero overlay.
why: Mask-free cell lattice at 100-200 nm pitch (smaller with smaller spheres) using a trough and RIE; shows an EUV-free hexagonal array path; risk is domain boundaries, mapped out as defect rows by BIST.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as capacitor molds
idea: First principle: high-AR plasma etch fights ion angular spread and neutral transport, but anodic Al2O3 pores grow by field-assisted dissolution at a pitch set by voltage (~2.5 nm/V) and keep going to any depth. Deposit ~3 um of Al over the storage-node contacts, seed pits with one imprint aligned to the contacts, and anodize at low voltage so the pores self-propagate straight down to AR >150:1; then line them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN by ALD.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and etch capex: no capacitor-hole mask and no high-AR mold etch; AR 150:1 at the same pitch gives ~2x Cs.

title: Self-healing capacitor dielectric via in-field oxygen-vacancy anneal
idea: First principle: high-k leakage tails come from mobile oxygen-vacancy clusters, which field and heat can redistribute. Add an array-level reverse-bias plus on-die microheater pulse (~300 C for microseconds) during idle that disperses vacancy clusters in ZrO2/HfO2, repairing weak cells in the field so the fab can relax its leakage-tail screen.
why: Leakage tail and yield (fact 3): fewer weak bits scrapped or fused out; longer refresh intervals.

title: Micro-banks: sixteen cells per printed bitline
idea: Minify the bitline to 16 cells and magnify the bank count to millions, each tiny sub-array with its own printed sense amplifier, so printed-wire RC drops about 64x.
why: Latency of printed memory: brings slow printed arrays toward ~100 ns access, trading area for speed on cheap area.

title: Treat DRAM fabs like dams: 30-year public depreciation
idea: Inverts 'fab capital must be repaid in five years'. A public infrastructure authority owns shell, utilities and long-lived tools (furnaces, wet benches, CMP), depreciated over 25-30 years, and leases capacity at cost to memory makers who own only the short-life leading-edge tools.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4); moving ~half of capex to 30-year life cuts wafer cost ~20-25% and speeds U.S. siting.

title: Vapor-liquid-solid growth builds vertical access channels upward instead of etching
idea: Effect: eutectic-droplet (VLS) epitaxy. Al or Sn catalyst dots (CMOS-safe, not Au) on buried bitlines grow epitaxial Si nanowires; the liquid droplet confines growth to a 10-15 nm vertical channel already aligned to its bitline, which then gets a gate-all-around wrap for 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM.
why: Fact 4: 4F2 cuts cell area 33% versus 6F2 without a node shrink; channel diameter is set by catalyst volume rather than litho, and the damaging HAR pillar etch disappears.

title: Capture and regenerate the 95% of ALD precursor that misses wafers
idea: First principle: ALD uses one monolayer per cycle, so ~95-99% of Hf, Zr and Ru precursor flows to the exhaust or the chamber walls. Fit each ALD exhaust with a cold-trap or sorbent cartridge that captures unreacted metal-organic precursor, and return the cartridges to the precursor maker to be regenerated into fresh precursor.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (Hf, Ru) and opex: ~5x less precursor purchased; recycled by design.

title: Ship it unrepaired: the host controller does the repair
idea: Reverse who repairs: remove laser fuses, redundancy rows and much of the repair test from the die; ship with an on-die defect map read at boot and let the memory controller remap bad rows like an SSD flash translation layer.
why: Saves 3-5% die area, the laser-repair tool set and test time, and raises usable yield; test is ~10% of DRAM cost.

title: Electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 ink for low-leakage access devices
idea: Magnify off-state resistance by printing electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 nanosheet inks (1.8 eV gap) as the access transistor channel, so leakage is low enough for long retention.
why: Refresh: wide-bandgap printed channels cut leakage far below the 13 fA tail, stretching refresh intervals on cheap printed arrays.

title: Liquid-nitrogen operation turns logic gain cells into seconds-retention memory
idea: Ideal: a transistor that never leaks, so no capacitor is needed. Closest: run capacitorless 2T/3T Si gain cells made in standard logic fabs at 77 K in LN2-cooled memory sleds, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by >10^6 and retention rises from ~50 us to seconds.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: memory from logic fabs with zero added masks; refresh nearly vanishes; cryocooler energy is the trade, offset by lower wire resistance.

title: Slow-light silicon-nitride delay-line memory from depreciated photonics fabs
idea: Revive the mercury delay line as coupled-resonator slow-light silicon-nitride waveguides (group index ~50-100) made in depreciated 200 mm photonics fabs with i-line litho and 1-2 masks: 64 WDM channels at 50 Gbaud recirculate through an on-chip amplifier and retimer, and data is tapped as it passes. It serves bandwidth-hungry, capacity-poor sequential buffers such as activation staging.
why: EUV dependence and capital (Fact 4): ~2 masks on 200 mm tool sets worth ~1% of a DRAM fab, replacing leading-edge SRAM buffers; density is only ~1 Mb/cm2, so the gain is capital per unit bandwidth, not cost per bit.

title: GaN-on-silicon power fabs build wide-bandgap 1T1C memory
idea: Revive the 1980s compound-semiconductor dynamic memory experiments (GaAs/AlGaAs charge storage with very long retention) using enhancement-mode p-GaN-gate transistors as access devices: the 3.4 eV gap and heterojunction confinement can push off-current far below silicon's, with MIM capacitors added in a short BEOL. Production uses depreciated 150/200 mm GaN-on-Si power-device lines.
why: Fact 3 and capital: refresh intervals of minutes instead of 32-64 ms, made in GaN fabs (several in the U.S.) at ~1-5% of DRAM-fab capex; at 0.25-0.5 um rules density is 10-30x below DRAM, so the first use is refresh-free capacity tiers.

title: Qimonda's trench DRAM resurrected by metal-assisted chemical etching
idea: Infineon/Qimonda's trench DRAM lost to stacked capacitors around 2009 because plasma etching of silicon trenches beyond ~AR 70 became impossible. Metal-assisted chemical etching (a catalyst mesh sinking into Si in HF/H2O2) reaches AR >100 in a room-temperature wet bench, so sink buried capacitors before the transistors using a self-aligned, non-gold catalyst grid stripped before gate oxidation.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR 115+ via wet chemistry instead of $10M+ etch tools; capacitor-module capex down ~10x.

title: Restart mothballed 2x-nm lines for stacked capacity-tier memory
idea: Worse: insist that all supply comes from leading-node fabs. Flip: buy idle, fully depreciated 300 mm lines (old DRAM, logic or NAND) and run a simplified 25-30 nm, zero-EUV DRAM. Stack 8-16 dies into CXL far-memory modules, where $/GB matters more than density per die.
why: Capital intensity: near-zero depreciation keeps $/bit competitive despite ~3-4x larger cells; online in 12-18 months on U.S. soil.

title: Silicon-carbide refresh-free memory in idle EV power-device fabs
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the same 150/200 mm 4H-SiC lines that make EV MOSFETs (overbuilt in the U.S. as EV demand slowed) produce 1T1C memory, since SiC's 3.26 eV gap suppresses thermal generation so strongly that SiC MOS storage cells have shown retention extrapolating to years at room temperature.
why: Zero refresh, built on existing U.S. i-line/DUV tools with near-zero new capex; density is ~50-100x below DRAM, so it serves persistent, edge and high-temperature tiers and frees mainstream DRAM for hot data (U.S. manufacturability, capital).

title: Self-assembled nanocrystal monolayer forms storage nodes without patterning
idea: Ideal: storage nodes that place themselves. Closest: a spin- or Langmuir-Blodgett-assembled monolayer of 5 nm Ru nanocrystals over a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide on the transistor channel; each cell gate overlaps ~20 dots that hold charge (ms retention, ns direct-tunneling write at ~1.5 V), with no lithography for the nodes.
why: Facts 1 and 4: no capacitor; storage-node formation is a single coating step; direct tunneling instead of Fowler-Nordheim avoids oxide wear and targets high endurance.

title: Neural pruning: over-grown random nanowire mesh carved into addressable cells
idea: Brains over-wire and then prune; solution-grow a dense random mesh of ~10 nm oxide-semiconductor nanowires between two orthogonal coarse electrode grids, then use electroforming pulses to burn out shorts and weak paths, characterize the surviving junctions on-die and address them through a learned map stored in a small SRAM table.
why: Self-assembled junctions far denser than the coarse lithographed grids give ~10x bits/mm2 using only relaxed ArF masks, if surviving-junction yield stays above ~30% (fact 4).

title: Substitute ballroom cleanrooms with sealed tool-to-tool mini-environments
idea: Build the fab as a sealed transport network where pods dock tool-to-tool under nitrogen, with ISO-1 cleanliness only inside tools and AMHS tubes, so the building itself is an ordinary ISO-8 warehouse.
why: Capital: cleanroom construction, HVAC and make-up air are ~20-30% of fab capex and a major energy/water load; could cut building capex ~2/3 and build time by about a year.

title: Revive defunct DRAM makers' process IP in idle 300 mm lines
idea: Po: dead companies make memory. License documented flows from defunct DRAM makers (e.g., buried-wordline 4x-nm processes) and transplant them into idle U.S. 300 mm logic/foundry lines whose 193i, ALD and CMP tools already exist, producing mature DDR4/LPDDR4 parts.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: skips ~5 years of process development; output in 2-3 years at a fraction of greenfield capex.

title: Backside-illuminated photoelectrochemical etch digs 150:1 trench capacitors in n-silicon
idea: Effect: photoelectrochemical macropore growth (Lehmann). In n-Si under anodic bias in HF, only holes photogenerated by backside light reach the pore tips, so pores grow straight to AR 150:1 from pits printed by i-line litho. A ~$40k PTFE cell with an LED array and potentiostat on 150 mm wafers demonstrates deep-trench DRAM capacitors within 24 months.
why: Fact 1: reaches AR far beyond 115 with a $40k tool instead of a $10M cryo etcher; fits embedded, legacy-node and chiplet DRAM at >=200 nm pitch, a niche the U.S. can manufacture.

title: Laser-CVD wafer repair of interconnect opens, borrowed from displays
idea: First principle: an open in an upper metal line is just ~10^9 missing atoms, which laser-induced chemical vapor deposition can add precisely, as LCD panel lines are repaired today. After wafer probe, locate opens and shorts in the top metal and redistribution layers, then write or cut them at laser-CVD and ablation stations.
why: Yield and capital per good die: part of the yield loss becomes repair; repairable by design.

title: Brody-style stencil metallization replaces litho for DRAM top metals
idea: Revive T. Peter Brody's 1973 first active-matrix display, built without photolithography by evaporating each layer through aligned metal shadow masks: deposit DRAM's coarse upper metals, pads and redistribution (>=1-3 um) by thermal or e-beam evaporation through reusable silicon-nitride stencils. Each stencil serves thousands of wafers, with no resist, develop, etch or argon sputter.
why: Fact 4 and capital: removes ~4-6 of DRAM's ~50-60 mask passes with their tracks, scanners and etchers (~10% of litho spend); evaporation needs only vacuum. Risks are stencil clogging and alignment at 300 mm.

title: Origami artist: roll one flat DRAM membrane into twenty tiers
idea: An origami artist turns a flat sheet into volume. Pattern one 2D cell array on a strained bilayer nanomembrane (e.g., SiN/SiGe) over a sacrificial layer; on release, built-in strain rolls it into a tight Swiss roll of ~20 turns, so one 2D lithography pass yields 20 tiers, with wordlines running along the roll and contacted at its edge.
why: Gets 3D density (fact 2) from 2D lithography, avoiding 26-tier stack deposition and deep etch; litho cost per bit falls ~1/N with N turns. Speculative: turn-to-turn registration, heat removal, edge contacts.

title: LTPS laser crystallization with argon-fluoride light for silicon-only tiers
idea: Borrow the phone-display LTPS line: deposit amorphous Si per tier and melt-crystallize it with a line-beam excimer laser using sequential lateral solidification for cell-sized grains; use ArF instead of the usual XeCl so even the laser gas is abundant, and the heat stays in the top ~50 nm so dozens of tiers stack without disturbing lower ones.
why: 3D DRAM (fact 2) with only Si: no In/Ga oxide semiconductors and no SiGe epitaxy; Gen-8-proven annealers; tier cost is about one deposition plus one anneal.

title: Kirkendall voiding hollows solid pillars into double-sided cylinder capacitors
idea: Effect: nanoscale Kirkendall effect. Fill capacitor molds with solid Co or Ni pillars and sulfidize them: metal diffuses outward faster than sulfur diffuses inward, leaving a hollow tube. An H2 reduction and a thin TiN overcoat then make both inner and outer walls electrode area. This drops the double-sided cylinder flow's support-mesh litho, mold strip and extra liner deposition.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: ~1.8x electrode area at the same AR, so AR 60 behaves like ~105, and 3-5 fewer steps per capacitor module.

title: Volumetric 3D printing: one holographic exposure defines electrode-plus-support lattice
idea: Like volumetric resin printers that cure a whole part at once, expose a 2 um-thick resist with four-beam interference to cure a 3D lattice of vertical posts with horizontal support bridges in one shot, then ALD-replicate it and burn out the resist to leave the capacitor bottom-electrode skeleton with built-in anti-leaning supports.
why: Facts 1 and 4: one exposure replaces mold deposition, support-mesh litho/etch steps and the HAR etch; built-in supports allow AR>100.

title: Substitute plasma etch with metal-assisted chemical etching for vertical silicon pillars
idea: Pattern a Pt or Au catalyst mesh (lift-off or block-copolymer), then immerse the wafer in HF/H2O2: silicon under the catalyst dissolves and the mesh sinks straight down, carving vertical-channel-transistor pillars or buried-wordline trenches at >100:1 with no ion damage and no bowing; the catalyst is stripped and reclaimed.
why: Facts 2 and 4: a 50-wafer wet batch replaces $5-10M cryo/HAR etch chambers; damage-free sidewalls also shrink the GIDL leakage tail (fact 3). Metal contamination control is the main risk.

title: Metal digs the hole: catalyst-assisted chemical etching
idea: Reverse plasma-from-above into catalyst-from-below: put Au/Ag catalyst dots (patterned by DUV or dewetting) on silicon and let metal-assisted chemical etching sink them downward, carving 200:1 vertical trench capacitors at room temperature in a wet bench.
why: Capacitor charge wall and etch-tool capex: AR 200:1+ without cryo plasma tools or EUV, giving ~2-3x Cs per cell.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D antifuse stack made rewritable with selector-charged capacitors
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D poly-diode antifuse memory (bought by SanDisk in 2005) stacked cheaply at ~4 masks per layer but died for being write-once. Keep the stacked poly pillar process and swap the antifuse for a small planar MIM capacitor charged through a bidirectional punch-through n-p-n selector, giving 1S1C dynamic cells with unlimited endurance, refreshed like DRAM.
why: Meets 100x: no access transistor, no high-AR capacitor, 8-16 DUV decks; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: selector leakage forces ms-scale refresh, higher refresh power, thin sense margin.

title: Arizona panel-level fan-out replaces TSV stacks for HBM bandwidth
idea: Scale from wafer to 600 mm panels: thin DRAM dies are placed face-down side by side on panels with ~1.5 um-line RDL made on domestic 1X panel steppers, routing ultra-wide buses laterally to the accelerator instead of through TSV stacks.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6: 3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss); square panels use ~90% of area vs ~60% for round wafers.

title: IBM Millipede's tip-wear killer removed by non-contact charge-writing probes
idea: IBM's Millipede thermomechanical probe storage died on tip wear, slow thermal writes and cheap flash. Hover a million-tip MEMS array ~5 nm above an unpatterned ferroelectric film, write bits by polarization-switching voltage pulses with no contact or heat, and read each bit by piezoresponse through per-tip front-ends.
why: Meets 100x: medium cost ~0 and MEMS made at ~1 um litho; est. ~$0.05/GB. Trades: us-ms seek, mechanical scanner and shock sensitivity, so it serves as a bulk tier behind DRAM.

title: Multi-head embroidery: write the one added layer maskless per die
idea: Because only one layer is added, write it with a 10,000-beam e-beam direct writer, like a multi-head embroidery machine stitching many garments at once; the mask becomes a data file that changes per product, per lot, or per die to route row and column repair without laser fuses.
why: Mask cost/time: zero reticle spend ($0.5-1M per critical mask), day-scale design turns, and fuse-free per-die repair that lifts yield.

title: Probe-less wafer test: on-die BIST powered and read optically
idea: Worse: test every die on multimillion-dollar ATE with slow probe-card touchdowns. Flip: put a tiny photovoltaic cell and an LED/photodiode link on every die. Flood-illuminate the wafer so all dies self-test with on-die BIST at once and report pass/fail and repair maps optically in parallel.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost; massively parallel optical test cuts tester capex and test time ~5-10x.

title: Fab-scale noble-gas fractionation recovers helium, neon and xenon
idea: First principle: helium, neon, krypton and xenon are chemically inert, so consuming them is a design choice. Route every tool exhaust to a fab-level cryogenic separation and membrane plant that recovers >90% of the noble gases and reinjects purified gas, with tools standardized to closed-loop gas ports.
why: Helium chokepoint and neon risk: 80-90% less purchased He; protects uptime and price.

title: Piezo lighter: sputtered AlScN ferroelectric made in U.S. RF-filter fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'piezo lighter' -> ferroelectric AlScN (Pr >100 uC/cm2) is deposited by plain reactive sputtering at <400 C, as in the BAW filter fabs of U.S. RF companies. It is used as the storage element of 1T1C non-volatile cells, and its giant Pr gives enough signal charge from a planar, non-pillar capacitor.
why: Non-volatile. It eliminates the high-AR capacitor mold and the ALD tools (facts 1 and 4) and reuses U.S. RF sputter capacity. Endurance (~1e7 today) needs a DRAM cache front and materials work.

title: Coral strain-templating: each tier self-assembles directly atop the last
idea: New coral polyps settle on the old skeleton; use the vertical correlation seen in stacked quantum dots: tier N's buried metal nodes leave a periodic strain and surface-energy imprint through a ~10 nm spacer that pins the block-copolymer or nanoparticle self-assembly defining tier N+1's features exactly above them. Only the first tier is lithographed.
why: If replication fidelity holds, 12-16 tiers cost one critical litho plus a cheap coat/anneal per tier, ~10x bits/mm2 at near-planar wafer cost and no EUV beyond tier 1 (fact 4).

title: Net weaver: aligned carbon nanotube periphery transistors above the array
idea: A net weaver lays parallel threads. Align solution-sorted semiconducting carbon nanotubes (>99.99% pure) into dense parallel arrays by dose-controlled floating evaporative self-assembly at room temperature, making CMOS periphery transistors (polarity set by contact work function) in tiers above the cell array at <=200 C.
why: Puts fast periphery above the array instead of beside it, reclaiming much of the 49% periphery area with no high-temperature step. High risk: residual metallic tubes, and alignment uniformity at 300 mm.

title: Vertical thyristor RAM revived inside the 4F² pillar
idea: Revive T-RAM and Kilopass's vertical-layered thyristor RAM (abandoned ~2010-2017): build a pnpn latch in the same vertical silicon pillar that 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM already etches, with a gated base for fast set and reset. The bistable thyristor holds data with a small standby current, so no storage capacitor is formed.
why: Fact 1 and capital: deletes the capacitor module (high-AR etch, high-k ALD, top plate) for ~15-20 fewer steps and about one EUV layer. Risks are standby current and temperature sensitivity.

title: One logic die multiplexes periphery for four bonded array dies
idea: Ideal: periphery costs nothing. Closest: leave only bitline sense amps and local drivers on array dies, and move decoders, I/O, DLL, refresh and ECC logic to one 28 nm logic die that time-multiplexes four stacked array dies through fine-pitch hybrid bonds.
why: Fact 7: periphery is ~49% of the die; sharing it 1:4 cuts total silicon per bit ~30-35% and moves logic to cheaper non-DRAM fabs.

title: Sixteen-fold spacer multiplication on a 1990s KrF stepper
idea: Inverts 'resolution belongs to the scanner'. Print 360 nm-pitch lines on a KrF stepper and run four rounds of sidewall-spacer transfer (LPCVD nitride/oxide spacers plus RIE), each halving pitch, to reach ~22 nm-pitch array lines with no overlay-critical steps.
why: Modern array pitch from fully depreciated litho; ~5-10x lower litho capex per dense layer (fact 4); line-edge roughness and cut layers are the limiters.

title: Repurpose idle SiC power fabs for ultra-low-leakage DRAM
idea: Worse: let EV-slowdown SiC fabs idle while DRAM is scarce. Flip: build 1T1C DRAM on 150/200 mm 4H-SiC wafers in existing SiC fabs. The 3.2 eV bandgap cuts generation leakage by orders of magnitude (1990s SiC DRAM cells held charge for hours), so refresh nearly vanishes, and the lower density is accepted for capacity tiers.
why: Refresh (fact 3) plus capital: reuses sunk U.S. SiC capacity (NC, NY) and needs no Si crucibles.

title: Exfoliate device layers, reuse the donor wafer fifty times
idea: First principle: a DRAM device needs about 1 um of single-crystal Si, so 99.9% of a 775 um wafer is just a mechanical carrier. Transfer 1 um device layers by hydrogen-implant cleaving or controlled spalling from a premium donor onto handles made of recycled Si, then re-polish and reuse the donor 30-50 times.
why: Scarce resources (quartz crucibles, polysilicon) and cost: up to ~30x less CZ crystal per wafer; the substrate is recycled by design.

title: Printed electric double-layer storage capacitors
idea: Magnify areal capacitance about 1000x by printing an ionic-gel film whose electric double layer (~10 uF/cm2) stores the bit's charge in a tiny planar footprint.
why: Capacitor charge wall: fF-scale charge in sub-um2 area with no pillar; the open risk is ion response time at ns speeds.

title: Etch passivation engineered to become the contact insulating liner
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: the sidewall passivation that storage-node-contact etch deposits (normally stripped by wet cleans) is tuned with SiCl4/O2 into a dense 2-3 nm SiOx-rich film and kept as the contact-to-bitline insulating liner, skipping the separate liner ALD and spacer etch.
why: Removes ~2-3 deposition/etch/clean steps per contact module and the cleaning damage to fine features (process steps).

title: Cell-stamp e-beam: a million shaped beamlets each write one cell
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x massively parallel e-beam with a programmable aperture plate shaped to the cell motif. Because the array is a lattice, each of ~1e6 beamlets is shaped into the same cell feature (parallel character projection) and the stage scan makes each beamlet write its own sub-array tile, so there are no masks and shot count falls by orders of magnitude vs pixel writing.
why: Mask cost and EUV dependence (fact 4); periodicity attacks e-beam's throughput problem; target 20-40 wafers/hour per column cluster at ~$30-50M; risk is beamlet uniformity and stitching.

title: Display demura for DRAM: ship per-die retention maps, relax specs
idea: Borrowed from OLED panels, which are cheap only because every pixel's mura is measured and a correction table is burned into the driver: at wafer probe, record each die's weak-row retention map (a few KB), store it in module SPD/flash, and have the controller refresh weak rows fast and strong rows 4-8x slower, so fabs can ship die with looser leakage specs; firmware and test software fit a small team.
why: Facts 3/4: a relaxed leakage-tail spec raises yield and skips process tightening; refresh energy drops ~50-70%.

title: Thermally drawn fibers shrink a macro-preform into memory
idea: Inverts 'small features need lithography'. Machine a centimetre-scale preform with interleaved metal, glass and semiconductor channels laid out as a capacitor-plus-channel array, then draw it in a fiber tower (~10,000x cross-section reduction) to 50-100 nm features over kilometres; slice into chiplets and stack.
why: Litho-free nanoscale features from 1970s-90s fiber towers; extreme capital efficiency if channel crystal quality and contacts can be solved.

title: Rental car: standalone MRAM modules from existing U.S. eMRAM foundry lines
idea: Random stimulus 'rental car' (use someone else's fleet now) -> STT-MRAM modules (CXL/DIMM) are taped out on embedded-MRAM processes already qualified at U.S. 22 nm foundry lines, using spare BEOL capacity with no new fab.
why: Near-zero capex and immediate U.S. manufacturability. Density is ~10-20x below DRAM, so it serves as a bridge tier for persistent metadata, KV caches and checkpoints, freeing DRAM bits during the shortage.

title: Shared EUV hub exposes critical layers for many small DRAM fabs
idea: Ideal: EUV is free for small makers. Closest: a central EUV hub exposes only the 5-7 critical layers of wafers shipped in sealed N2 FOUPs from several smaller DRAM fabs that do all DUV, deposition and etch locally, with tolling priced per layer.
why: Fact 4 and capital: $200-380M scanners are pooled at high utilization; a new entrant skips EUV capex, roughly -30% entry capital.

title: Helium-free etch: hydrogen backside cooling plus closed-loop recapture
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out separates the needed property (wafer-to-chuck heat conduction) from the scarce substance: switch electrostatic-chuck backside gas from He to H2 or H2/Ar where process-tolerant, and fit remaining He users with membrane plus cryogenic recapture loops reclaiming >90% of backside and purge flow.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium has been offline since March 2026; fab He use drops 70-90%, removing a shutdown risk for etch and ALD tools (scarce resource, throughput).

title: Remanufacture retired hyperscaler DIMMs for 30-year industrial spares
idea: Extreme user: industrial plants that need DDR4 spares decades after launch. Run a line that strips DRAM packages from 5-6-year-old retired server DIMMs (DRAM barely wears out), retests and bins them, then rebuilds them onto new PCBs with fresh PMICs and SPD data.
why: Supply with no fab capital: millions of GB per year return to use at a fraction of new-bit cost and energy.

title: Thin-tunnel charge-trap 3D NOR DRAM built in idle NAND fabs
idea: Box: nitride-trapped charge behind a 1.5-2 nm tunnel oxide x vertical poly-Si channel in parallel NOR strings x current sensing x 200+ word-plane stack x Si x existing 3D NAND toolset. The thin tunnel oxide trades retention (seconds) for 10-50 ns writes, refreshed like DRAM, while NOR wiring gives random access; staircase, channel-hole and replacement-gate modules are reused unchanged.
why: Capital and time: converts already-depreciated NAND capacity into DRAM-class capacity without a new $15B fab, density from tiers not litho; risk is trap endurance (~1e10) vs DRAM's unlimited, requiring a DRAM cache in front.

title: Vertical codewords across tiers break 3D DRAM yield compounding
idea: Combine 3D NAND-style tier stacking with tier-orthogonal coding: each codeword takes one symbol from each of ~32 tiers along the vertical bitline, so a defective tier (lateral-transistor shorts, capacitor voids) costs only one symbol per codeword. Per-tier yield can then be 99% rather than 99.99%.
why: Tier-yield compounding is a hidden blocker for 26+ tiers (fact 2). Relaxed per-tier yield permits faster deposition, fewer inspections and ~2x more tiers per stack.

title: Block copolymer quadruples a sparse capacitor-hole lattice
idea: Constraint: print only one in four capacitor holes. Sparse ArF guide posts at twice the pitch template a cylinder-forming block copolymer by graphoepitaxy, which self-assembles the missing hexagonal holes at ~24 nm pitch; the minority cores are removed and transferred into the mold.
why: Fact 4: replaces EUV or SAQP for the densest hole layer; 4x density multiplication from a cheap mask, about one fewer EUV layer.

title: ZettaCore redox molecules turn squat capacitors into full-charge cells
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin molecular memory folded around 2008 because the molecules could not survive 400 C back-end steps and needed all-new circuits. Use them only as a charge multiplier: graft a redox monolayer (~1e14 molecules/cm2, ~160 fC/um2) onto the storage-node electrode after all hot steps, so an AR~8 cylinder stores the ~2.5 fC an AR~70 cylinder holds today.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and deletes the hardest high-AR mold etch and its tool fleet; capacitor-module tool hours fall ~5-10x.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten in buried wordlines
idea: Worse: keep 80%-China tungsten in every buried wordline, contact and plug. Flip: switch to fluorine-free, barrierless Mo CVD sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines; Mo has lower resistivity than W at thin dimensions.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint removed; ~20-30% lower wordline RC also permits thinner, denser lines.

title: Alignment-free capacitor carpet: cells harvest random nanorod capacitors
idea: Po: the capacitor ignores the transistor. Make a dense random carpet of isolated vertical nanorod capacitors (diameter smaller than the gap between storage-node pads) in an insulating matrix laid over the transistor array; each landing pad simply collects whatever rods sit on it, so no capacitor litho or overlay is needed.
why: Capacitor litho/overlay (facts 1,4): removes the capacitor-hole patterning layer; summing ~10-50 rods per cell tightens the Cs distribution.

title: Myelin multilamellar self-assembly lays down twenty tiers in one coat
idea: Schwann cells wrap axons in dozens of uniform lamellae; spin a high-chi lamellar block copolymer that orders parallel to the substrate into 20+ layers (~12 nm period), then use sequential infiltration synthesis to turn one block into AlOx insulator and the other into In2O3 channel, creating a whole tier stack in one coat-anneal-infiltrate sequence below 200 C.
why: Tier-stack cost drops from ~100 depositions to one coat plus a few infiltration cycles; 40+ BEOL-compatible tiers with a single hole/slit patterning give ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat cost (facts 2, 4).

title: Clam growth-line oscillating bath deposits the whole tier superlattice nonstop
idea: Clam shells lay periodic growth bands from a self-oscillating cycle; engineer the spontaneous potential oscillations known in Cu/Cu2O electrodeposition so a single bath alternates metal wordline layers and oxide-semiconductor layers ~15 nm thick, forming 100 tier pairs in one run with no valve switching, vacuum or tool transfer.
why: Tier-stack deposition at wet-bench cost and tungsten-free; 100 tiers patterned once give ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat wafer cost (facts 2, 4, resources).

title: Snake-molt cleaving stacks forty single-crystal tiers from one donor
idea: A snake sheds a perfect thin copy of its skin each cycle; hydrogen-implant and cleave 30 nm single-crystal Si films from one reusable, repolished donor onto the growing stack with 20 nm oxide bonding interlayers, building 40 monocrystalline tiers, then pattern all tiers at once with one hole/slit etch and lateral recess.
why: Single-crystal lateral transistors fix the leakage tail that blocks 3D cells (facts 2, 3) with no Si/SiGe strain limit; 40 tiers patterned once give ~10x bits/mm2 while each tier adds only a bond/cleave/CMP cycle, keeping wafer cost near flat.

title: Sn: liquid-tin skin printing of 2D SnO p-channel periphery
idea: Touch a wafer to a liquid Sn-Ga alloy under controlled O2 so its self-limiting, atomically thin SnO surface skin transfers in one stroke over 300 mm; pattern it into p-type TFTs stacked above the array to host part of the decoder and sense-amp periphery.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49% of die): stacking periphery in BEOL layers made by a vacuum-free heated-bath tool (vs a ~$5M CVD) could reclaim 20-30% die area; complements n-type oxides from prior work.

title: Thylakoid grana: atom-thin 2D channel tiers stacked at 10 nm
idea: Chloroplasts stack thylakoid membranes into dense grana; alternate low-temperature MOCVD MoS2 monolayers with ~8 nm ALD insulator to build a 60-tier stack only ~0.6 um tall, then form vertical wordlines and bitlines once through it so each tier is a lateral gain-cell layer with a 0.7 nm channel and almost no off-state leakage.
why: A 10 nm tier pitch (vs ~50-60 nm for Si/SiGe) puts 60 tiers in the height of 10, so one shallow hole etch yields ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat cost and low refresh (facts 2, 3).

title: One vacuum cluster runs forty capacitor steps without queuing
idea: Collapse the wafer's timescale: a linear vacuum cluster integrates ~40 sequential deposition, etch and clean steps of the capacitor module, so the wafer never leaves vacuum or waits in a FOUP queue; the module goes from ~20 days to ~1 day of cycle time.
why: Cuts WIP inventory capital and queue-time defects; fewer transfers raise yield and total fab cycle time drops ~25%.

title: Substitute litho-etch pairs with area-selective bottom-up deposition
idea: Use small-molecule or SAM inhibitors that adsorb only on dielectric so ALD grows metal (or dielectric) only where wanted, forming landing pads and capacitor bottom contacts self-aligned to underlying features without a lithography and etch pair. Selectivity loss is reset with periodic deposition-etch supercycles.
why: Removes 2-4 edge-placement-limited masks and their etch/clean steps per wafer and raises overlay yield in the dense 6F2 contacts (fact 4).

title: Chef's pressure cooker: supercritical CO2 metal electrodes for deep holes
idea: A pressure cooker reaches where dry heat cannot. Deposit Ru, Cu or Ni electrodes from organometallic precursors dissolved in supercritical CO2 at ~150-250 C and ~15 MPa, reduced by H2 at the surface; the zero-surface-tension fluid coats the bottoms of 100:1+ holes and trenches evenly.
why: Gives conformal electrodes at AR >100 without high-temperature CVD TiN, enabling taller capacitors and fewer steps; scCO2 reactors are simple pressure vessels, cheaper than ALD clusters. Risks: precursor purity, carbon pickup, throughput.

title: Substitute 300 mm silicon wafers with Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build a capacity-tier DRAM (oxide-TFT access devices plus stacked MIM capacitors) on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in converted LCD/OLED fabs, patterning 40-60 nm features with panel-scale nanoimprint. One panel equals the area of ~70 300 mm wafers and the line tools are largely depreciated or idle.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: panel fabs cost 5-10x less per m2 processed; even at 4-8x lower density than DDR5, cost per bit could compete for cold/capacity tiers. Overlay on glass and TFT leakage are the risks.

title: Federated defect-image library compresses new-fab yield ramps
idea: Worse: every new fab learns its defects alone over 2-3 years. Flip: entrants and toolmakers feed inline SEM/optical defect images and parametric fails into a standardized defect taxonomy. Classifiers train federated (data never leaves each fab) and ship root-cause models and recipe corrections to new lines on day one.
why: Capital: ramp months burn depreciation (~55% of wafer cost); cutting the ramp from ~24 to ~10 months saves ~$1B+ per new fab.

title: TSV-free HBM: stack dies that talk by inductive coupling
idea: Reverse wires to fields: replace through-silicon vias with on-die inductive coil transceivers between thinned stacked dies, with power carried by a few large edge vias or the backside.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes TSV etch, liner, fill and CMP and their 20-30% yield loss, and could cut HBM area per bit toward DDR5 levels.

title: Inductive-coupling die stacking replaces Bosch-etched TSVs in HBM
idea: Extreme user: AI HBM stacks, whose TSVs are etched with SF6/C4F8 Bosch cycles. Pass data between stacked dies through on-chip coil pairs (near-field inductive links) and deliver power with a few large through-mold or edge conductors, so no fluorinated via etch is needed.
why: HBM TSV tax: frees the TSV keep-out area (much of the ~3x area penalty) and removes TSV yield loss and the fluorinated Bosch process.

title: Inductive coil links stack DRAM dies without any TSVs
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: stacked dies thinned to <20 um talk through on-chip spiral coils and receive power through heavily doped silicon columns, so there are no TSV etch/fill/reveal steps, no microbumps and no metallurgical joints to grow intermetallics over a decade at 125 C.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV area and yield tax (~3x area per bit, -20-30% yield) and several back-end tool types.

title: Float-glass panel interposers made in idle display fabs
idea: Retool underused Gen-6 LCD/OLED backplane lines (each panel ~40 wafers of area) to make 2 um line glass-core interposers and redistribution panels for memory-logic packages, using their existing steppers, sputter and plating, and replacing silicon CoWoS-style interposers for HBM/LPDDR stacks.
why: Fact 6 and capital: unlocks interposer capacity that gates HBM shipments using amortized panel fabs at ~1/5-1/10 the cost per area of 300 mm silicon interposers.

title: IBM eDRAM trench sold as merchant pre-capacitored substrate wafers
idea: IBM's deep-trench eDRAM died when its single in-house SOI process ended with GlobalFoundries' 7 nm exit. Disaggregate it: a substrate vendor (Soitec-style) mass-produces blank wafers with a uniform grid of deep-trench capacitors, and any fab, including U.S. legacy logic fabs, builds access transistors and periphery on top aligned to that grid.
why: Capital: moves the deepest etch and high-k module into one specialized high-throughput substrate fab; lets non-memory fabs make DRAM-class memory; ~30% of DRAM process steps outsourced to a shared, fully utilized line.

title: Defect-absorbing soft-remap arrays that tolerate cheaper patterning
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: make the address map flexible instead of the process perfect - each 1 Mb mat carries ~3% spare rows/columns and an on-die CAM that remaps failing 64-cell groups at test and in the field, so the fab can run older ArF immersion scanners with ~1.5x worse overlay and accept cell-defect rates near 1e-4.
why: Older DUV tools and relaxed overlay specs cut litho capex ~50% on several layers and lift yield; ~3-5% area buys the tolerance (facts 4, 7).

title: Periphery from U.S. mature foundries bonded to array-only wafers
idea: Worse: build sense amps and logic in the same costly DRAM process that compromises both. Flip: make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab, buy the periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from a 28/22 nm U.S. foundry, and hybrid-bond the two wafer-to-wafer at sub-micron pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): DRAM fab bit output per tool rises ~1.6-1.9x, using underused U.S. mature-node capacity.

title: Cu: hybrid-bond DRAM arrays to periphery from depreciated US fabs
idea: Make only the cell array in the leading-edge DRAM fab and fabricate the periphery (~49% of die) on 28-40 nm logic wafers in existing, depreciated U.S. foundries, joining the two with Cu-Cu hybrid wafer bonding.
why: Facts 4 and 7: roughly doubles array bits per expensive DRAM wafer and uses idle U.S. capacity with near-zero new capex for the periphery half.

title: T-RAM rebuilt as stacked back-end oxide thyristors
idea: T-RAM's thyristor cell died needing SOI and fighting temperature-sensitive leakage in silicon. Build the p-n-p-n latch from low-temperature deposited oxides (p-type SnO or Cu2O over n-type IGZO) in back-end layers, where wide bandgaps cut thermal leakage by orders of magnitude, using one via-sized mask per tier and stacking 8 tiers above the periphery.
why: Removes SOI and front-end area; a bistable latch needs no refresh (recovers ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth); 8 BEOL tiers give ~8x bits per mm2 without any EUV layer.

title: 2050 atomic inkjet: maskless spatial-ALD print heads write periphery wiring
idea: A 2050 engineer prints atoms like ink. Micro-nozzle spatial-ALD heads confine precursors and a local micro-plasma in a ~10 um gap to deposit oxide and metal only where the head passes, writing periphery wiring and pads (~1-5 um lines) directly at <=250 C with no mask, resist or etch.
why: Removes coat/expose/develop/etch/strip (5-7 steps) on coarse layers, perhaps ~30% of all patterning steps, using cheap modular heads. High risk: throughput and micron-scale resolution.

title: Core memory reborn as colloidally patterned magnetic vortex nanorings
idea: Ferrite core memory died because cores were hand-threaded and millimetre-sized, yet its coincident-current selection made a passive crossbar with no sneak paths. Pattern magnetic vortex nanorings with mask-free nanosphere lithography (a self-assembled bead monolayer) over a coarse X/Y/sense line grid, so only rings under full coincident field switch and several rings per crossing vote.
why: Meets 100x: no transistor per bit, litho-free ring formation, unlimited magnetic endurance and non-volatility; est. ~$0.1/GB at 8 decks. Trades: destructive read-and-restore like core, high write currents, small inductive read signal.

title: Light-addressed electrodeposition prints periphery metal from a DMD projector
idea: Effect: photoconductivity. In a plating bath, a DMD projector lights a photoconductive a-Si:H or TiO2 seed layer, making only the lit pixels conductive, so copper deposits in the projected pattern with no mask or resist. $150k of optics plus ~$700k of development reaches 1-2 um lines for periphery and redistribution layers in 24 months.
why: Facts 6 and 7 and masks: maskless metal for periphery and packaging RDL cuts mask and litho cost for low-volume U.S. DRAM and fast design spins.

title: Vicinal-wafer atomic steps template sub-15 nm wordline lines
idea: Ideal: the crystal itself is the mask. Closest: anneal a miscut Si surface so atomic steps bunch into a periodic ridge array with a 10-20 nm period set by the miscut angle; area-selective deposition decorates the step edges into a hardmask for wordline lines across the whole wafer, with one DUV cut mask for line ends.
why: Fact 4: dense line/space with zero EUV and none of SAQP's 10+ deposition/etch loops; pitch is set by crystallography, not optics.

title: VLSI-Project-style consortium builds non-EUV DRAM patterning tools
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where rival DRAM makers co-funded lithography and tool R&D and then competed: form a U.S. DRAM tool consortium funded per wafer start that develops e-beam projection, imprint and X-ray tools aimed at DRAM's periodic arrays, with IP pooled among members.
why: Capital intensity and EUV single-supplier risk: shares ~$2-4B of tool R&D across members and targets the 5-7 EUV layers behind depreciation's ~55% share of wafer cost.

title: In-situ leach mining: copper-catalyzed wet etching of deep holes
idea: As in-situ leaching dissolves ore where it lies, use metal-assisted chemical etching: copper catalyst dots (instead of Au/Ag) defined by imprint or self-assembly on silicon sink vertically in HF/H2O2, digging capacitor holes or vertical channels beyond 100:1 at room temperature in a wet bench.
why: Deep-etch capex and EUV (facts 1, 4): ~10x cheaper tools, unlimited AR, no plasma damage, no W-doped or thick carbon hardmask. Risks: catalyst wander and Cu contamination control.

title: Drawn nanochannel glass gives billion-hole capacitor templates
idea: Worse: create capacitor holes one etch step at a time at AR 75:1. Flip: stack and redraw glass rods with etchable cores again and again (nanochannel glass has reached ~30 nm channels) into plates of uniform hexagonal channels beyond 100:1. Etch out the cores, ALD the electrodes and dielectric, and bond a thin-film transistor layer on top.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR above 100 comes free from drawing, with no plasma etch; glass is U.S.-made.

title: Farmer's co-op grain elevator: shared toll-EUV hub for new fabs
idea: Farmers don't each own a grain elevator. A neutral co-op owns a cluster of 4-6 EUV scanners sited among several new U.S. memory fabs (start-ups, IDMs, national labs); sealed FOUP shuttles carry wafers to the hub for their EUV layers only, members pay per exposure, and capacity shares are owned like co-op stock.
why: Takes the ~$1B EUV ticket off each new entrant, so a 20k wafer/month fab can start with DUV-only capex, and lifts EUV utilization from ~70% to >90%. Risks: logistics, contamination, and ~1-2 days of queue time per pass.

title: Accumulative roll bonding: 3D DRAM tiers from repeated layer transfer
idea: Metallurgy builds nanolaminates by repeatedly rolling and folding; build 3D DRAM tiers by hydrogen-implant smart-cut transfer of 30-50 nm single-crystal Si sheets onto an oxide-bonded stack, then bond stack to stack to double tiers each round (8 to 16 to 32 to 64), instead of growing a 100+ layer Si/SiGe superlattice.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): avoids the strain-relaxation limit on epi stack height, gives monocrystalline channels in every tier, and reaches 64 tiers in ~6 bond rounds.

title: Rotary spatial ALD deposits capacitor dielectrics at 300 wafers per hour
idea: Constraint: one-tenth of today's deposition tool count. Wafers orbit under separated precursor and purge zones near atmospheric pressure, so ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 stacks grow by motion rather than valve cycling; long-dwell and ozone-assisted sectors restore conformality in 70:1 holes.
why: ALD is a growing slice of capex, especially for 3D DRAM's dozens of ALD steps; ~10x throughput per tool, ~-70% module capex.

title: Nano hemispherical-grain roughening boosts capacitor area without litho
idea: Revive the 1990s hemispherical-grain (HSG) polysilicon trick that roughly doubled 64 Mb capacitor area by seeding amorphous silicon until it beaded into grains: apply it to the walls of 3D-DRAM lateral capacitors, where there is more room, using LPCVD SiH4 seeding in H2/N2 to form 3-5 nm grains, then convert them to TiN or silicide electrodes.
why: Fact 1: 1.5-2x electrode area per footprint raises Cs without taller structures; LPCVD furnaces batch 100+ wafers on hydrogen and nitrogen with no rare gas. Risk is grain bridging in narrow gaps.

title: Oyster's trick: hydrothermal perovskite capacitor dielectric grown at 150 C
idea: A marine biologist notes that shells grow ceramics in cold seawater. Line the capacitor holes with ALD TiO2, then convert it in place to crystalline SrTiO3 or BaTiO3 by hydrothermal reaction in Sr(OH)2/Ba(OH)2 solution at 120-200 C, skipping the 600-700 C crystallization anneal.
why: Targets k ~70-150 (fact 1 needs k ~70), raising Cs without more AR, in a wet bath rather than anneal tools, and suits stacked tiers. High risk: crystallinity below 8 nm, leakage, and carbonate contamination.

title: Metallized-film capacitor self-clearing: aluminum plates that isolate shorts
idea: Film capacitors survive breakdowns because their thin Al electrode vaporizes around a fault; make the DRAM cell plate a thin Al-Ti film and apply a wafer-level clearing pulse, so a plate-to-node pinhole short burns open locally and becomes one dead cell (handled by ECC) instead of a shorted plate that kills a whole mat or chip.
why: Yield, redundancy and periphery (fact 7): lets dielectrics thin for more Cs without mat-level yield loss and cuts repair rows; Al replaces W/TiN plate fills.

title: Eliminate resist and etch: imprinted inhibitor molecules steer area-selective ALD
idea: Nanoimprint a monolayer of ALD-inhibitor molecules (e.g., alkylsilane SAMs) in the negative pattern, then grow the film only where it is uninhibited, so the layer is patterned additively in one deposition with no resist coat, exposure, develop, etch or strip.
why: Collapses a ~5-tool, 8-12 step patterning loop into 2 steps for semi-critical layers; applied to ~15 layers it trims fab tool count ~10% and cuts chemistry and water per layer.

title: Load-sharing magnetic matrix switch moves row decoding into package
idea: Revive the 1950s load-sharing matrix switch, the core-era decoder in which a few binary drive lines threaded through a pattern of transformers excite exactly one output: build it as coupled planar transformers in the organic package substrate so 10 binary-weighted primaries select one of 1,024 wordline-group drivers. The DRAM die keeps only local wordline drivers; global row predecode transistor trees leave the litho die.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (Fact 7): moving global decode off-die could recover ~5-10% die area and several periphery-only implant/metal masks, with the decoder made on ~$50M substrate lines instead of in a $15B fab. Risk is pulse fidelity of GHz transformer coupling.

title: Brewery-to-sanitizer conversion: 3D NAND lines build vertical gain cells
idea: Like distilleries switching to hand sanitizer, convert a 3D NAND line during gluts: keep its stack deposition, channel-hole and slit masks and tools, swap the charge-trap fill for an IGZO channel, and add exactly one mask that splits each hole's gate ring into separate write and read gates, forming a 2T0C vertical gain-cell string.
why: Capital/time: DRAM-class bits from existing NAND capacity in months rather than 3-5 years, for +1 mask on an amortized flow.

title: Transistor-free crosspoint: printed threshold selector plus capacitor
idea: Minify the cell to 4F2 by printing crossed wordlines and bitlines, with a volatile Ag-filament threshold switch in series with a planar capacitor at each crossing as the access device.
why: Density and process steps: no transistor layers in the array, so 2-3 printed layers make a full array.

title: Printed memory prize: 1 GB per square meter
idea: Minify entry capital with a US milestone prize (target: 1 GB per m2 at under $5/m2 and 100 ns latency) tied to a shared open roll-to-roll pilot line where teams rent web time by the meter.
why: US manufacturability and capital: dozens of teams can try printed DRAM approaches without each building a line.

title: Tunnel-etched electrolytic-capacitor aluminum foil becomes DRAM capacitor plate
idea: Worse: plasma-etch every capacitor hole into hard crystal. Flip: borrow the electrolytic-capacitor industry's DC tunnel etching, which in seconds drills straight crystallographic <100> tunnels above 50:1 into Al foil. Seed the tunnel sites with a pattern, coat them with ALD high-k and a top electrode, and use the foil itself as the common plate.
why: Capacitor wall plus capital: wet electrochemical etch at $/m2 cost replaces high-AR plasma etchers.
